section_summaries.epidemiology: Lymphatic filariasis (LF) is a mosquito-transmitted nematode infection, primarily caused by Wuchereria bancrofti (over 90% of infections) and less commonly by Brugia malayi and B. timori. It is endemic in 52 countries, with 856 million people at risk and an estimated 100 million infected, predominantly in South and Southeast Asia (65%) and sub-Saharan Africa (30%). The distribution is highly focal due to varying mosquito vector behaviors, with Anopheles, Culex, Aedes, and Mansonia species serving as vectors. Microfilariae of W. bancrofti and B. malayi exhibit nocturnal periodicity, circulating in peripheral blood between 10 PM and 2 AM, coinciding with vector feeding times. LF used to be endemic in North America, Australia, China, Japan, and Korea but has since been eliminated in many areas, though increasing urbanization presents new challenges for control.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: LF is caused by adult nematodes (W. bancrofti, B. malayi, B. timori) residing in human lymphatics, leading to damage and dysfunction. Adult female worms release microfilariae that circulate in the blood. Mosquitoes ingest microfilariae, which develop into infective third-stage larvae (L3) over 10-14 days. These L3 larvae are deposited in the human dermis during feeding, migrate to lymphatics, and mature into adult worms in 6-9 months. Adult worms, 20-100 mm long, cause massive dilation of lymphatics, valvular dysfunction, and impaired interstitial fluid removal. Death of adult worms and associated inflammation (acute filarial lymphangitis) can accelerate lymphatic dysfunction. The accumulation of adult worms in lymphatics, particularly in the lower extremities, axillary nodes, and male genitalia, determines the type and extent of clinical disease. W. bancrofti and Brugia species rely on an obligate intracellular bacterial endosymbiont, Wolbachia, for survival, embryogenesis, and molting.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: LF presents a spectrum from subclinical infection to chronic, disabling manifestations. Most infected individuals are asymptomatic despite having circulating microfilariae or filarial antigens, though underlying lymphatic damage, microscopic hematuria, or proteinuria may be present. Acute manifestations include acute filarial lymphangitis (AFL), caused by adult worm death, presenting as painful inflammation progressing distally along lymphatic vessels, and acute dermatolymphangioadenitis (ADLA), caused by bacterial super-infection in dysfunctional lymphatics, presenting as reticular inflammation with severe pain, fever, and chills. Brugian filariasis can cause local abscesses. Chronic manifestations, affecting 25-30 million people, include hydrocele (most common in W. bancrofti-infected men), lymphedema and elephantiasis (particularly in lower extremities, arms, breast, and penis/scrotum), graded by WHO into four stages. Chyluria, a rare but serious manifestation from ruptured retroperitoneal lymphatics, leads to chyle loss and malnutrition. Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE), caused by W. bancrofti or B. malayi, results from an exaggerated allergic response to microfilariae in pulmonary blood vessels, characterized by nocturnal cough, wheezing, fever, eosinophilia, elevated IgE, and interstitial lung infiltrates. Travelers typically experience AFL rather than chronic disease.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Definitive diagnosis of LF relies on detecting the parasite, parasite antigen, or parasite DNA, especially considering epidemiologic history and clinical findings. The gold standard is microfilariae detection on a thick blood film stained with Giemsa or hematoxylin. For W. bancrofti and B. malayi, blood samples are collected between 10 PM and 2 AM due to nocturnal periodicity. Circulating filarial antigen (CFA) detection using rapid-format immunochromatographic test strips is the most widely used method for W. bancrofti, being semi-quantitative and more sensitive than microfilariae detection. Antibody-based assays, particularly for anti-filarial IgG4, indicate active infection but cannot distinguish between active and prior infections or different filarial species. PCR-based assays are research-based for detection in blood and xenomonitoring. Ultrasound can detect motile adult worms in lymphatics. Differential diagnoses for acute manifestations include bacterial infection, thrombophlebitis, or trauma. For chronic lymphedema, malignancy, post-operative changes, congenital malformations, hereditary lymphostasis, renal or cardiac failure, and podoconiosis should be considered. Sexually transmitted infections should be considered for orchitis and epididymitis.
section_summaries.treatment: Treatment involves single-dose combination regimens to reduce microfilarial and circulating antigen levels. The WHO recommends diethylcarbamazine (DEC, 6 mg/kg), ivermectin (200 µg/kg), and albendazole (400 mg) for mass drug administration (MDA), except where onchocerciasis or loiasis are co-endemic. DEC is active against microfilariae and can sterilize adult worms, but has adverse events related to rapid microfilarial killing; co-infections with onchocerciasis or high levels of L. loa microfilariae must be excluded due to severe reactions. Ivermectin is highly active against microfilariae and contributes to adult worm sterilization, with fewer adverse events in onchocerciasis co-infection, but is not recommended for high L. loa microfilarial counts. Albendazole has no microfilarial activity but some against adult worms, leading to a slow decline in microfilariae over months, and is safe for onchocerciasis/loiasis co-infection. Doxycycline (200 mg daily for 8 weeks) targets Wolbachia endosymbionts, causing long-term sterility and eventual death of adult worms, and improves lymphatic pathology; it's contraindicated in children <9 and pregnant/breastfeeding women. For advanced lymphedema, medication cannot reverse the disease, but basic lymphedema management (e.g., hygiene, elevation) can reduce fevers and improve symptoms.
section_summaries.prevention: The global program to eliminate lymphatic filariasis (GPELF), launched in 2000, aims to interrupt transmission through mass drug administration (MDA). MDA regimens include ivermectin/DEC/albendazole (for non-onchocerciasis/loiasis co-endemic areas), ivermectin/albendazole (for onchocerciasis co-endemic Africa), or albendazole alone (for loiasis co-endemic Africa). Four to six rounds of MDA are typically required to reduce microfilaria reservoirs to levels that interrupt transmission, although new triple-drug regimens may shorten this. For travelers and short-term residents, bed nets and mosquito repellants are recommended, as transmission is inefficient and requires prolonged exposure. Malaria control efforts, including bed nets, also impact LF transmission in co-endemic areas.
